front: What are the six edge sources used to classify every strategy?
back: Speed, liquidity provision, structural/regulatory, informational, behavioral and risk premium. Each strategy sits on two axes: holding horizon and edge source. (02-strategies/index.md)

front: Which edge sources dominate short horizons, and which dominate long ones?
back: Short horizons: liquidity provision, speed and structure. Long horizons: risk premia and behavioral effects. Informational edges sit in the middle. (02-strategies/index.md)

front: Why is most "stat arb" described as liquidity provision on a slower clock?
back: Because you are mostly paid for absorbing other investors' temporary price pressure, the same service a market maker sells, held for days instead of seconds. (02-strategies/index.md)

front: If you remember one row of a strategy dossier's header table, which should it be?
back: "Counterparty: who pays and why they accept it." A strategy is a claim that someone will keep paying you; no identifiable payer is a red flag. (02-strategies/index.md)

front: Formula: breakeven cost per dollar traded, and net alpha?
back: c* = gross alpha / turnover; net alpha = alpha - turnover x cost. Example: 12% gross alpha at 60x turnover breaks even at 20 bp; each extra bp of cost costs 0.6% a year. (02-strategies/how-quants-evaluate-a-strategy.md)

front: Why does a small haircut to gross alpha hurt high-turnover strategies so much?
back: Net alpha is gross minus turnover x cost. In the illustrative intraday stat-arb case (25% gross, 500x turnover) breakeven is 5 bp and each extra bp of cost costs 5% a year. (02-strategies/how-quants-evaluate-a-strategy.md)

front: What is the marginal-Sharpe hurdle for adding a strategy to a book?
back: It improves the book only if its Sharpe exceeds rho x the book's Sharpe, where rho is its correlation to the book. A mediocre uncorrelated strategy often beats a brilliant clone. (02-strategies/how-quants-evaluate-a-strategy.md)

front: Number: a Sharpe-1.5 clone with correlation 0.8 is offered to a Sharpe-2.0 book. Optimal weight?
back: Zero: its hurdle is 0.8 x 2.0 = 1.6, above 1.5, so the book stays at 2.00. An uncorrelated Sharpe-0.8 strategy lifts it to 2.15 (illustrative). (02-strategies/how-quants-evaluate-a-strategy.md)

front: How is a new strategy typically funded, and what can live P&L prove?
back: In stages (shadow, small capital, ramp) with kill criteria written before the first trade. Months of live P&L cannot prove alpha; they can prove the implementation. (02-strategies/how-quants-evaluate-a-strategy.md)

front: Spot the error: "Behavioral edges rarely die; they just compress when capital floods in."
back: That describes risk premia. Behavioral edges (under-reaction, extrapolation) are arbitraged down by publication and crowding. (02-strategies/how-quants-evaluate-a-strategy.md)

front: How does a speed edge die, according to the six-edge-source table?
back: Through a winner-take-most arms race: everyone but the fastest is priced out. Latency differences always exist somewhere, so the edge persists for the leader. (02-strategies/how-quants-evaluate-a-strategy.md)

front: Equity market making: who pays, and why do they accept it?
back: Impatient liquidity demanders (execution algos, rebalancers, routed retail) pay the half-spread for immediacy, because waiting costs more in drift and leakage. Informed traders and latency arbitrageurs win; uninformed flow pays for them. (02-strategies/a-liquidity-provision/equity-market-making.md)

front: Number: Menkveld (2013) per-trade economics of one HFT market maker?
back: EUR 0.88 gross per trade: a EUR 1.55 net spread less a EUR 0.68 loss on positions; gross Sharpe 9.35 (Dutch stocks 2007-2008, academic case study). (02-strategies/a-liquidity-provision/equity-market-making.md)

front: Roughly what is a US equity market maker's net margin per share, and the industry pool?
back: About a tenth of a cent per share; US equity market making nets roughly $1-3B a year industry-wide (both [Estimate]). (02-strategies/a-liquidity-provision/equity-market-making.md)

front: Which algorithm cards are core to equity market making?
back: M2 fair value and microprice, M4 quoting and inventory control, M5 adverse selection and markouts, M6 queue position, M7 hedging, M9 algorithmic risk controls. (02-strategies/a-liquidity-provision/equity-market-making.md)

front: Spot the error: "A market maker's edge is mostly its quoting formula."
back: The edge is fair value, speed (cancelling stale quotes in time) and cost per share, more than the formula. Lab 05: adverse selection cut an optimal quoter from $95 to $42 an hour (synthetic). (02-strategies/a-liquidity-provision/equity-market-making.md)

front: How does equity market making fail?
back: Adverse-selection spikes, technology errors (Knight Capital, over $460M in 45 minutes, 2012), volatility events, factor exposure, and tick and fee rule changes. (02-strategies/a-liquidity-provision/equity-market-making.md)

front: Why is Sharpe on capital not meaningful for equity market making?
back: It is P&L-limited, not capital-limited: little capital, huge turnover (Menkveld's firm traded 1,397 times per stock per day). Virtu's IPO filing showed one losing day in 1,238. (02-strategies/a-liquidity-provision/equity-market-making.md)

front: What does an ETF market maker quote around?
back: Its own fair value built from the basket, futures and correlated ETFs: hedge cost plus a small margin. Inventory is hedged at once and netted at the close by creation or redemption. (02-strategies/a-liquidity-provision/etf-market-making.md)

front: Number: Flow Traders' 2025 ETP margin?
back: EUR 485.8M of net trading income on EUR 1,940bn of ETP value traded, about 2.5 bps [Reported]. Margins are thin and scale is concentrated. (02-strategies/a-liquidity-provision/etf-market-making.md)

front: When a bond ETF's basket is stale or its market shut (2020, Greece 2015), what does the market maker price?
back: The fund itself, not its NAV: the ETF becomes the price-discovery venue, so discounts to stale NAV are not necessarily mispricing. (02-strategies/a-liquidity-provision/etf-market-making.md)

front: ETF market making: who pays, and what is the signature failure?
back: Investors wanting a basket in one ticket and block traders buying immediate risk transfer. It fails when hedges cannot be priced: 24 August 2015 saw 1,058 LULD halts in 327 ETPs. (02-strategies/a-liquidity-provision/etf-market-making.md)

front: Options market making as an income statement?
back: Edge (price minus theo) is revenue; theta minus gamma is implied-versus-realized volatility; vega is a mark; hedging, fees and payment for order flow are costs. (02-strategies/a-liquidity-provision/options-market-making.md)

front: How does an options market maker hold its inventory?
back: As Greeks: delta hedged within seconds; gamma and vega warehoused and shaded away through quotes, all read off one fitted volatility surface. (02-strategies/a-liquidity-provision/options-market-making.md)

front: Numbers: retail share of US options volume, options PFOF share, and 0DTE share of SPX volume?
back: Retail over 60% of volume (Bryzgalova et al. 2023); options are two-thirds of all PFOF; 0DTE a record 66.2% of SPX volume in July 2026. (02-strategies/a-liquidity-provision/options-market-making.md)

front: Options market making: who pays?
back: Retail buyers of short-dated options (leverage, wide percentage spreads), institutions buying index puts and structured-product hedgers paying for size; covered-call and put-write funds sell volatility cheaply. (02-strategies/a-liquidity-provision/options-market-making.md)

front: How does options market making fail?
back: On gaps and volatility spikes while short gamma: one session can erase weeks of theta. Also skew spikes, informed flow, pin and assignment, wing model error, runaway quoting. (02-strategies/a-liquidity-provision/options-market-making.md)

front: What is the edge in retail flow internalization?
back: Segmentation: an exchange prices for its average counterparty, while a wholesaler knows the broker and prices that flow. It pays PFOF, fills at or inside the NBBO and keeps a fraction of a cent. (02-strategies/a-liquidity-provision/retail-flow-internalization.md)

front: Number: how concentrated is US retail wholesaling?
back: Six wholesalers received over 90% of individual investors' marketable orders [Verified]; Citadel Securities claims about 35% of US-listed retail volume [Reported]. (02-strategies/a-liquidity-provision/retail-flow-internalization.md)

front: What does GameStop in January 2021 show about internalization?
back: When retail turns correlated, wholesalers internalize less: GameStop's off-exchange share of dollar volume fell from 62.6% to 32.8% in a week. (02-strategies/a-liquidity-provision/retail-flow-internalization.md)

front: Number: round-trip cost dispersion for identical retail orders across brokers?
back: 0.07% to 0.46% across six brokerage accounts [Verified], evidence that broker routing and segmentation matter. (02-strategies/a-liquidity-provision/retail-flow-internalization.md)

front: Closing-auction liquidity provision: who pays and why?
back: Index funds, ETFs and benchmarked managers that must trade at the official close: tracking error costs more than a few bps, so they concede price to whoever absorbs the imbalance. (02-strategies/a-liquidity-provision/auctions-and-closing-liquidity.md)

front: Number: growth of the US closing auction?
back: About 3.1% of dollar volume in 2010, a record 9.4% of notional in Q2 2024, about 20% on rebalance days; Nasdaq's cross printed a record $334B in June 2026. (02-strategies/a-liquidity-provision/auctions-and-closing-liquidity.md)

front: What evidence says auction liquidity provision earns a concession?
back: Bogousslavsky and Muravyev (2023): the closing price concession reverts quickly and almost completely on average. Edge per share is small; risk is overnight inventory and informed imbalances. (02-strategies/a-liquidity-provision/auctions-and-closing-liquidity.md)

front: Which line must an auction liquidity provider never cross?
back: Trading to move the close is manipulation. Offering the side that offsets a published imbalance is legitimate. (02-strategies/a-liquidity-provision/auctions-and-closing-liquidity.md)

front: What is latency arbitrage?
back: Trading against quotes left stale for microseconds after public news (a futures tick, a sweep elsewhere) moved fair value. Whoever reaches the matching engine first wins: a race, not a forecast. (02-strategies/b-speed-and-structural/latency-arbitrage.md)

front: Numbers from London Stock Exchange race data (Aquilina, Budish and O'Neill)?
back: Winners beat the first loser by a modal 5-10 microseconds; races were about 20% of FTSE 100 volume; the latency tax is about 0.5 bp of volume, roughly $5B a year globally. (02-strategies/b-speed-and-structural/latency-arbitrage.md)

front: Latency arbitrage: who pays?
back: Sniped quoters pay first; investors pay last through wider spreads. Quoters keep quoting because uninformed flow still pays on average. (02-strategies/b-speed-and-structural/latency-arbitrage.md)

front: Why is latency arbitrage said to be about rank, not capital?
back: Profits track latency rank (Baron et al. 2019): the fastest firm earns, the runner-up near zero. Speed bumps such as IEX's blunt it on one venue only. (02-strategies/b-speed-and-structural/latency-arbitrage.md)

front: Where is price discovered first for US large caps, and where does it propagate?
back: In E-mini futures, the cheapest, most levered instrument, then to ETFs, constituents and ADRs (Hasbrouck 2003). (02-strategies/b-speed-and-structural/lead-lag-and-cross-asset-arbitrage.md)

front: Lead-lag arbitrage: the trade in one sentence?
back: Price each follower from beta-weighted leader moves, take stale quotes or skew your own, and hedge in the leader. (02-strategies/b-speed-and-structural/lead-lag-and-cross-asset-arbitrage.md)

front: Number: how did futures-to-cash lead-lag windows change 2005-2011?
back: They shrank from about 100 ms (2005) to single-digit milliseconds (2011). At seconds to minutes it becomes a statistical forecast with more capacity. (02-strategies/b-speed-and-structural/lead-lag-and-cross-asset-arbitrage.md)

front: Which three trades tie one index exposure together?
back: ETF vs basket (creation and redemption), futures vs basket (carry), and ETF vs constituents (statistical). (02-strategies/b-speed-and-structural/etf-and-index-arbitrage.md)

front: What is the no-arbitrage band, and Lab 07's size for it?
back: The cheapest arbitrageur's all-in cost; trade inside your own band and you lose. Lab 07: about +/-7.4 bps on average, up to 14.9 bps in stress (synthetic lab result). (02-strategies/b-speed-and-structural/etf-and-index-arbitrage.md)

front: ETF and index arbitrage: who pays, and when does it fail?
back: Hurried ETF traders and leveraged longs paying implied financing in futures. It fails when the basket cannot be traded: halts, closed markets, capacity limits. (02-strategies/b-speed-and-structural/etf-and-index-arbitrage.md)

front: Maker-taker versus inverted venues?
back: Maker-taker: takers pay up to the 30-mil access-fee cap and makers earn a rebate. Inverted: makers pay to post (buying queue priority at the same displayed price) and takers earn a small rebate. (02-strategies/b-speed-and-structural/fee-and-microstructure-driven-strategies.md)

front: Fee- and microstructure-driven strategies: what is legal and what is not?
back: Fee and queue optimization is legal; spoofing, layering and wash trades are not. (02-strategies/b-speed-and-structural/fee-and-microstructure-driven-strategies.md)

front: How would the SEC's 2024 tick and fee package affect fee-driven strategies, and when?
back: The 10-mil cap and half-penny tick would compress rebate and queue edges, but compliance is delayed to the first business day of November 2027 [Verified]. (02-strategies/b-speed-and-structural/fee-and-microstructure-driven-strategies.md)

front: Where and when did stat arb begin?
back: At Morgan Stanley in the early-to-mid 1980s (Bamberger's industry-group reversal system, scaled by Tartaglia's group) and at Princeton-Newport; D. E. Shaw, founded 1988, carried it into hedge funds [Reported]. (02-strategies/c-statistical-arbitrage/stat-arb-overview-and-history.md)

front: Number: how did crowding erode a simple contrarian strategy (Khandani and Lo)?
back: Average daily return fell from 1.38% (1995) to 0.13% (2007), needing about 9:1 leverage to match 1998; it lost 6.85% unlevered in three days of August 2007. (02-strategies/c-statistical-arbitrage/stat-arb-overview-and-history.md)

front: What does a modern stat-arb book look like?
back: 1,000-3,000 names, factor-neutral, 1-10 day holds, many signals, a cost-aware optimizer; capacity roughly $0.5-5B gross per book [Estimate]. (02-strategies/c-statistical-arbitrage/stat-arb-overview-and-history.md)

front: Pairs trading: two ways to choose pairs?
back: Distance: smallest sum of squared differences of normalized prices over a 12-month formation period (Gatev, Goetzmann and Rouwenhorst 2006); or cointegration tests (Engle-Granger, Johansen). (02-strategies/c-statistical-arbitrage/pairs-trading-and-cointegration.md)

front: Number: Gatev, Goetzmann and Rouwenhorst (2006) results?
back: Up to 11% a year before costs over 1962-2002; top-20 pair returns fell from 118 to 38 bps a month after 1988. After realistic costs, largely unprofitable since 2002. (02-strategies/c-statistical-arbitrage/pairs-trading-and-cointegration.md)

front: Why is pair selection the hard part? (Lab 08)
back: Multiple testing: of same-sector pairs passing a 5% cointegration test, about 94% were false, and Benjamini-Hochberg kept none (synthetic lab result). (02-strategies/c-statistical-arbitrage/pairs-trading-and-cointegration.md)

front: Pairs trading: who pays, and when does the trader pay instead?
back: Investors trading one stock for reasons unrelated to its twin (liquidations, index deletions, block sales). When the gap is news, the counterparty is informed and the pairs trader pays. (02-strategies/c-statistical-arbitrage/pairs-trading-and-cointegration.md)

front: Spot the error: "Stop-losses are a source of alpha in pairs trading."
back: Stops are insurance, not alpha. A broken relationship costs about a period's profit; stops cap that damage. (02-strategies/c-statistical-arbitrage/pairs-trading-and-cointegration.md)

front: Avellaneda and Lee (2010): the recipe?
back: Strip returns of 15 PCA eigenportfolios (or sector ETFs), fit residuals as an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, trade when |s-score| > 1.25. Net of 10 bps round trip: Sharpe 1.44 (1997-2007), 0.9 (2003-07). (02-strategies/c-statistical-arbitrage/factor-residual-mean-reversion.md)

front: Number: Lab 09's factor-residual book, gross versus net?
back: Turnover 57x a year; gross Sharpe 3.0 becomes 0.63 net at $10M and -2.20 at $100M; break-even cost 9.7 bps per dollar traded (synthetic lab result). (02-strategies/c-statistical-arbitrage/factor-residual-mean-reversion.md)

front: Factor-residual mean reversion: who pays?
back: Price-insensitive liquidity demanders: rebalancing or redeeming funds, index and ETF flows, liquidations. A mandate or deadline makes a few bps of slippage acceptable. (02-strategies/c-statistical-arbitrage/factor-residual-mean-reversion.md)

front: Factor-residual reversion: core algorithms and failure modes?
back: P1 risk models, P2 covariance shrinkage, D3 signal transforms, P3 MVO, P5 cost models. Fails via crowded unwinds, cost overruns, factor leakage and news-driven residuals that drift. (02-strategies/c-statistical-arbitrage/factor-residual-mean-reversion.md)

front: Which papers established short-term cross-sectional reversal, and why does it pay?
back: Lehmann (1990), Jegadeesh (1990), Lo and MacKinlay (1990). It is a fee for absorbing temporary price pressure; expected returns rise with the VIX (Nagel 2012). (02-strategies/c-statistical-arbitrage/short-term-cross-sectional-reversal.md)

front: Number: decay of the French 1-month reversal factor's gross Sharpe?
back: 0.92 in 1963-1991, 0.15 in 1992-2026, 0.01 in 2010-2026; it lost 18% in 2025. It survives residualized, news-filtered and inside multi-signal books. (02-strategies/c-statistical-arbitrage/short-term-cross-sectional-reversal.md)

front: Why does reversal have the highest gross and thinnest net Sharpe of classic anomalies?
back: Turnover of 50-100x a year (Lab 10: 90x) means costs decide everything; standalone net is about zero or below [Estimate]. (02-strategies/c-statistical-arbitrage/short-term-cross-sectional-reversal.md)

front: When does short-term reversal fail?
back: When liquidity providers all need liquidity at once: August 2007 and March 2020. Also cost-model error, news moves and momentum regimes. (02-strategies/c-statistical-arbitrage/short-term-cross-sectional-reversal.md)

front: What is the intraday U-shape?
back: Volume and volatility peak at the open and close; spreads are widest at the open. The closing auction alone prints roughly 5-10% of volume (2025). (02-strategies/c-statistical-arbitrage/intraday-patterns-and-seasonality.md)

front: What is market intraday momentum?
back: The day's return up to 3:30 p.m. predicts the last half hour, in 60+ futures markets (1974-2020), tied to dealers' and leveraged ETFs' gamma hedging. (02-strategies/c-statistical-arbitrage/intraday-patterns-and-seasonality.md)

front: How do firms mostly monetize intraday patterns?
back: As execution timing and ML features, not standalone bets; standalone net Sharpe is now about 0.3-0.8 [Lore]. (02-strategies/c-statistical-arbitrage/intraday-patterns-and-seasonality.md)

front: ML-driven short-horizon alpha: how good is each prediction, and where does the money come from?
back: Each barely beats a coin flip (rank IC 0.01-0.05). Breadth across thousands of stocks makes the money; costs take most of it, so they belong in the objective. (02-strategies/c-statistical-arbitrage/ml-driven-short-horizon-alpha.md)

front: What are the hard parts of ML short-horizon alpha?
back: Labels, purged validation, retraining and resisting overfitting, more than model choice. Failures come from regime breaks, crowded unwinds and backtests that learned noise. (02-strategies/c-statistical-arbitrage/ml-driven-short-horizon-alpha.md)

front: Number: academic ML stat arb on the S&P 500 (1992-2015)?
back: Over 0.45% a day before costs, shrinking over time; an LSTM variant reported a gross Sharpe of 5.8 [Reported]. Practitioner net at scale: 1-2 [Lore]. (02-strategies/c-statistical-arbitrage/ml-driven-short-horizon-alpha.md)

front: The mid-frequency cross-sectional equity pipeline, in order?
back: Raw alphas, transforms (winsorize, rank or z-score), neutralization, combination, risk model, optimizer with a cost model, trades. (02-strategies/d-mid-frequency-alpha/cross-sectional-alpha-and-neutralization.md)

front: How does the Fundamental Law explain cross-sectional book design?
back: IR is about TC x IC x sqrt(breadth). Each alpha is barely better than a coin flip (daily IC 0.005-0.05), so the edge must come from many nearly independent bets. (02-strategies/d-mid-frequency-alpha/cross-sectional-alpha-and-neutralization.md)

front: Why is a cross-sectional book's capacity limited to roughly $1-10B GMV?
back: Under square-root impact, total cost grows like size^1.5 while alpha grows like size, so costs overtake alpha past some size [Estimate]. (02-strategies/d-mid-frequency-alpha/cross-sectional-alpha-and-neutralization.md)

front: Fact: what did WorldQuant say about Kakushadze's 101 Formulaic Alphas (2016)?
back: 80 of the 101 alphas were in production when published [Verified]. (02-strategies/d-mid-frequency-alpha/cross-sectional-alpha-and-neutralization.md)

front: Core families of fundamental quant signals?
back: Value (B/M, E/P, EV/EBITDA), profitability (gross profits / assets), accruals, asset growth and earnings-quality composites, ranked within sector. (02-strategies/d-mid-frequency-alpha/fundamental-quant-signals.md)

front: What is the hard part of fundamental quant, and why is capacity high?
back: The data: point-in-time availability, reporting lags and restatements. Capacity is $1-20B+ because turnover is about 1-3x a year versus 25-100x for daily books [Estimate]. (02-strategies/d-mid-frequency-alpha/fundamental-quant-signals.md)

front: What is PEAD, and the original magnitude?
back: Post-earnings announcement drift: buy positive surprises, short negative ones, hold weeks. Bernard and Thomas (1989): about 4.2% over 60 trading days, top minus bottom decile, 1974-1985. (02-strategies/d-mid-frequency-alpha/earnings-and-event-driven.md)

front: Is PEAD still alive?
back: Contested: Martineau (2022) finds it gone in non-microcaps since 2006; 2025 papers dispute that. The question is open. (02-strategies/d-mid-frequency-alpha/earnings-and-event-driven.md)

front: Why is merger arbitrage described as a short put?
back: It earns a small spread if the deal completes and loses heavily if it breaks; academic excess return about 4% a year net of transaction costs, 1963-1998. (02-strategies/d-mid-frequency-alpha/earnings-and-event-driven.md)

front: Why does analyst revision momentum work?
back: Analysts update slowly and in herds, so consensus revisions are serially correlated and prices drift after them; investors anchored on stale estimates pay. (02-strategies/d-mid-frequency-alpha/analyst-revisions-and-sentiment.md)

front: What do short interest and days-to-cover read, and what is the catch?
back: The footprints of informed short sellers. The same crowded shorts are the squeeze candidates. (02-strategies/d-mid-frequency-alpha/analyst-revisions-and-sentiment.md)

front: Number: decay of the S&P 500 inclusion effect?
back: Additions averaged +7.4% in the 1990s but under 1% in the 2010s (Greenwood and Sammon 2025). Rules are public, so crowding shrinks the effect and pulls it earlier. (02-strategies/d-mid-frequency-alpha/flow-driven-strategies.md)

front: Number: what do index funds pay for predictable reconstitution trading (Petajisto)?
back: At least 21-28 bp a year for S&P 500 funds and 38-77 bp for Russell 2000 funds, 1990-2005. (02-strategies/d-mid-frequency-alpha/flow-driven-strategies.md)

front: Flow-driven strategies: who pays and why?
back: Index funds that must trade at the effective-day close and value tracking error over price; pensions on calendar rules; redeeming funds; mechanically hedging dealers. (02-strategies/d-mid-frequency-alpha/flow-driven-strategies.md)

front: What is alternative data mostly used for?
back: Nowcasting a company's numbers before it reports, mostly revenue ahead of earnings, from card, app, web, satellite, location, job-posting and supply-chain data. (02-strategies/d-mid-frequency-alpha/alternative-data.md)

front: Where is the edge in alternative data?
back: In the plumbing: panel-bias correction, ticker mapping, as-delivered history and backfill detection. Edges shrink as vendors add clients. (02-strategies/d-mid-frequency-alpha/alternative-data.md)

front: Number: satellite parking-lot counts around retailer earnings?
back: About 4-5% in the three days around earnings, 2011-2017 [Reported]. (02-strategies/d-mid-frequency-alpha/alternative-data.md)

front: What binds first in alternative data, and an example?
back: Legal review: MNPI and provenance, scraping law, privacy. App Annie paid a $10M SEC penalty in 2021. Most buyers spend $0.5-2.5M a year on data [Reported]. (02-strategies/d-mid-frequency-alpha/alternative-data.md)

front: The three clocks of text signals?
back: Machine-readable news (seconds to days), earnings-call tone (days to weeks), filing changes (months; Lazy Prices earned up to 188 bps a month, 1995-2014). (02-strategies/d-mid-frequency-alpha/nlp-and-llm-signals.md)

front: What is the signature backtest trap for LLM signals?
back: Pretraining look-ahead: a model trained on text through year Y has read what happened next. Time-stamped models suggest it is modest but real. (02-strategies/d-mid-frequency-alpha/nlp-and-llm-signals.md)

front: Lopez-Lira and Tang (JFE 2026): main finding?
back: LLM headline scores predict next-day returns, and the edge shrinks as adoption rises. (02-strategies/d-mid-frequency-alpha/nlp-and-llm-signals.md)

front: Factor model lineage from CAPM?
back: CAPM, Fama-French 3 (1993), Carhart 4 (1997), Fama-French 5 and the q-factor model (2015). Each step re-labels yesterday's alpha as beta. (02-strategies/e-risk-premia-and-factors/factor-investing-fundamentals.md)

front: Number: gross Sharpe of single US factors versus a mix (1963-2026, French library)?
back: HML 0.34, momentum 0.50, RMW 0.37; an equal-risk mix 0.71, but only 0.23 over 2007-2026. Diversification across factors is where the Sharpe comes from. (02-strategies/e-risk-premia-and-factors/factor-investing-fundamentals.md)

front: The factor zoo debate in one line?
back: One camp says most of 400+ anomalies fail honest tests, another that most replicate; both find published returns shrink by about half. (02-strategies/e-risk-premia-and-factors/factor-investing-fundamentals.md)

front: Three reasons a factor can pay?
back: A risk premium, a persistent behavioral mispricing, or a structural constraint on others (e.g., leverage limits behind low beta). (02-strategies/e-risk-premia-and-factors/factor-investing-fundamentals.md)

front: Define 12-1 momentum and its original return.
back: Buy the past year's winners, short its losers, skipping the latest month. About 1% a month over 1965-1989 (Jegadeesh and Titman 1993); it outlived publication. (02-strategies/e-risk-premia-and-factors/momentum.md)

front: When do momentum crashes happen, with two examples?
back: In sharp rebounds after bear markets, when high-beta losers rally: -74% in July-August 1932 and -49% in March-May 2009. (02-strategies/e-risk-premia-and-factors/momentum.md)

front: Number: what does volatility scaling do to momentum?
back: Roughly doubles the Sharpe: 0.45 to 0.87 on the same 1927-2026 months (our replication), because crashes follow high-volatility states. (02-strategies/e-risk-premia-and-factors/momentum.md)

front: Momentum: turnover and capacity versus reversal?
back: Lab 10: 6.5x a year against reversal's 90x. Break-even capacity about $52B in the US (Frazzini, Israel and Moskowitz). Crowding is the price. (02-strategies/e-risk-premia-and-factors/momentum.md)

front: Spot the error: "Momentum's long-run gross Sharpe of about 0.5 still holds today."
back: Since 2000 the UMD factor's gross Sharpe is only 0.14 (0.41 volatility-scaled). (02-strategies/e-risk-premia-and-factors/momentum.md)

front: Why do value, quality and low volatility pay?
back: Value: distress and extrapolation. Quality: underpriced profitability. Low beta: leverage constraints push investors into high beta. Weak correlation makes the combination carry the Sharpe. (02-strategies/e-risk-premia-and-factors/value-quality-low-vol.md)

front: Number: value's worst run on record?
back: HML -58% from December 2006 to September 2020, then +68% to December 2022. Whether intangibles broke book value is still debated. (02-strategies/e-risk-premia-and-factors/value-quality-low-vol.md)

front: Long-run gross Sharpe ratios of value, profitability, QMJ and BAB?
back: Value (HML) 0.34, profitability (RMW) 0.37, quality-minus-junk 0.48, betting-against-beta 0.70. Since 2010: HML -0.06, BAB 0.76. (02-strategies/e-risk-premia-and-factors/value-quality-low-vol.md)

front: Two kinds of factor pain, and their defenses?
back: Fast crowded unwinds (August 2007, days) and slow premium droughts (the 2018-2020 quant winter, years). Responses: diversification, volatility targeting, bounded tilts, less-crowded variants, not heroic timing. (02-strategies/e-risk-premia-and-factors/factor-timing-crowding-and-quant-winters.md)

front: How is crowding measured?
back: Indirectly: short interest, comomentum, valuation spreads and prime-broker positioning data. (02-strategies/e-risk-premia-and-factors/factor-timing-crowding-and-quant-winters.md)

front: Spot the error: "Value-spread timing is a separate source of return from value."
back: Value-spread timing is largely more value; academic evidence ranges from little gain (Asness et al. 2017) to substantial (Haddad, Kozak and Santosh 2020). (02-strategies/e-risk-premia-and-factors/factor-timing-crowding-and-quant-winters.md)

front: Number: how much do index options overprice volatility (1990-2026)?
back: The VIX averaged 19.4 against 15.3 realized over the next 21 trading days and exceeded it on 86% of days (our computation from Cboe data). (02-strategies/f-volatility-and-derivatives/volatility-risk-premium-and-vol-arb.md)

front: What does a short-volatility payoff look like?
back: Many small gains, rare huge losses (monthly skewness near -6). It is crash insurance and pays like it: 2008, February 2018, March 2020, April 2025. (02-strategies/f-volatility-and-derivatives/volatility-risk-premium-and-vol-arb.md)

front: Why does the volatility risk premium persist, and how has it decayed?
back: Hedgers must buy protection and sellers face margin limits. Its CAPM alpha has shrunk toward zero since about 2010. (02-strategies/f-volatility-and-derivatives/volatility-risk-premium-and-vol-arb.md)

front: What is a dispersion trade really betting on?
back: Index variance is roughly average stock variance x average correlation. Selling index vol and buying constituent vol is short implied correlation: a bet stocks move together less than options imply. (02-strategies/f-volatility-and-derivatives/dispersion-and-correlation-trading.md)

front: Number: implied versus realized correlation, S&P 500, 1996-2012?
back: Implied averaged 39.5% versus 32.5% realized, the gap shrinking after 2001. Driessen, Maenhout and Vilkov (2009): priced, but hard to harvest after frictions. (02-strategies/f-volatility-and-derivatives/dispersion-and-correlation-trading.md)

front: Why is dispersion short a crisis? Give the COR3M range.
back: Correlations spike when markets crash. Cboe's 3-month implied correlation index read 90 on 2020-03-16 and a record low 7.2 on 2026-07-10. (02-strategies/f-volatility-and-derivatives/dispersion-and-correlation-trading.md)

front: Define carry, with the one formula that covers all asset classes.
back: What a position earns if prices and curves do not move: (spot - futures) / futures. Rate differentials in FX, roll yield in commodities, yield plus roll-down in bonds. (02-strategies/g-futures-and-macro-context/carry-and-cross-asset-risk-premia.md)

front: Number: carry's gross Sharpe (Koijen, Moskowitz, Pedersen and Vrugt)?
back: About 0.7 per asset class and 1.1 diversified, 1972-2012 academic backtest. (02-strategies/g-futures-and-macro-context/carry-and-cross-asset-risk-premia.md)

front: What risk is carry paid for, with an example?
back: Crash risk: carry loses in every class at once in global recessions. AUD/JPY fell 46% in three months of 2008; the August 2024 yen unwind hit equities too. (02-strategies/g-futures-and-macro-context/carry-and-cross-asset-risk-premia.md)

front: What is time-series momentum (trend following)?
back: Go long futures that have risen and short those that have fallen, across 50-150 markets at equal risk, with 1-12 month lookbacks. (02-strategies/g-futures-and-macro-context/trend-following-and-ctas.md)

front: Trend following's payoff shape?
back: Convex: bleeds in chop, earns in long moves ("crisis alpha"), loses on V-shaped reversals. (02-strategies/g-futures-and-macro-context/trend-following-and-ctas.md)

front: Number: SG Trend Index live returns 2022-2026?
back: +27.4% in 2022, -4.2% in 2023, +2.4% in 2024 and 2025, +15.8% in 2026 to September [Reported]. Live returns trail backtests. (02-strategies/g-futures-and-macro-context/trend-following-and-ctas.md)

front: Evidence for trend following's persistence?
back: Persistence in all 58 futures Moskowitz, Ooi and Pedersen tested, and positive returns in every decade since 1880 [Verified]. (02-strategies/g-futures-and-macro-context/trend-following-and-ctas.md)

front: Strategy x algorithm matrix: which cards are the workhorses?
back: The cost model P5 (18 strategies), signal transforms D3 (15), risk models P1 (14) and signal evaluation D4 (14); 357 of 1,170 cells are filled. (02-strategies/h-cross-cutting/strategy-x-algorithm-matrix.md)

front: Into which three failure clusters do strategies group?
back: Crowded deleveraging (stat arb, mid-frequency, factors), short convexity (vol selling, dispersion, carry, options MM) and technology or rule changes (speed, market making). Diversify across clusters. (02-strategies/h-cross-cutting/strategy-comparison-matrix.md)

front: How does evidence quality vary with strategy speed?
back: Slow strategies' Sharpe ratios are [Verified] from decades of public data; fast strategies' are mostly [Lore]. (02-strategies/h-cross-cutting/strategy-comparison-matrix.md)

front: What engine drives most strategy failures in the failure gallery?
back: A feedback loop: losses force selling, selling moves prices, new prices force more selling. Leverage sets how fast it runs; liquidity sets how far prices go. (02-strategies/h-cross-cutting/strategy-failure-gallery.md)

front: Number: the August 2007 quant quake in Khandani and Lo's model?
back: Their model stat-arb strategy lost 6.85% over 7-9 August 2007 and made back 5.92% on 10 August. Survival depended on leverage and pre-agreed rules. (02-strategies/h-cross-cutting/strategy-failure-gallery.md)

front: LTCM 1998: leverage and loss?
back: About 30:1 balance-sheet leverage met a flight to liquidity; the fund was down 52% for the year by 31 August, followed by a Fed-brokered $3.6B private rescue. (02-strategies/h-cross-cutting/strategy-failure-gallery.md)

front: Flash Crash, 6 May 2010: magnitude and rule changes?
back: E-mini down 5%+ and SPY 6%+ in 4.5 minutes; 20,000+ trades broken. Then single-stock circuit breakers, stub-quote ban, the market access rule, LULD and new market-wide breakers. (02-strategies/h-cross-cutting/strategy-failure-gallery.md)

front: "Volmageddon", 5 February 2018?
back: Inverse VIX products rebalanced mechanically into a volatility spike: VIX +115.6% in a day, XIV -96%; XIV was terminated. (02-strategies/h-cross-cutting/strategy-failure-gallery.md)

front: The life cycle of a quant edge?
back: Discovery, early profits, publication and diffusion, crowding, decay or a crowded crash, then migration to a faster horizon, new data, new markets or more complex combination. (02-strategies/h-cross-cutting/evolution-of-quant-strategies.md)

front: What shrank in speed edges: profit per opportunity or the window?
back: The window (97 ms to 7 ms); profit per opportunity did not shrink, and the pool concentrated in the fastest few firms. (02-strategies/h-cross-cutting/evolution-of-quant-strategies.md)

front: Accounting lens on alpha from the evolution page?
back: Treat a signal as an amortizing intangible: research is maintenance capex, and a book that stops replacing alpha shrinks every year. (02-strategies/h-cross-cutting/evolution-of-quant-strategies.md)

front: Number: three strategies at Sharpe 1.0, 1.5 and 0.8 combined?
back: About 1.57 at equal risk and 1.64 at optimal weights (illustrative): a multi-strategy book earns its Sharpe mostly from low correlation, not precise weights. (02-strategies/h-cross-cutting/how-firms-combine-strategies.md)

front: Formula: ceiling on combining pods with Sharpe S and average pairwise correlation rho?
back: S / sqrt(rho): no number of pods can beat it. Crowding across pods raises rho and lowers the ceiling. (02-strategies/h-cross-cutting/how-firms-combine-strategies.md)

front: Pod shops versus centralized one-book quant funds?
back: Pods combine P&L streams from independent teams under central risk limits (talent, accountability, fast failure detection). One book combines signals into one forecast and optimizer, netting trades and constraints first. (02-strategies/h-cross-cutting/how-firms-combine-strategies.md)

front: Reported pod drawdown rules and pass-through costs at multi-managers?
back: Millennium reportedly halves a PM's capital at a 5% loss and is likely to part ways near 7.5%; pass-through expenses typically run 3-10% of net assets [Reported]. (02-strategies/h-cross-cutting/how-firms-combine-strategies.md)

front: Why is "what is their algorithm?" the wrong question about a quant firm?
back: A firm runs a pipeline of dozens of algorithms, each answering one narrow question. Better: "which stage of your pipeline is the binding constraint?" (03-algorithms/there-is-no-single-algorithm.md)

front: Name the five canonical US equity quant pipelines.
back: The HFT market-making loop, short-horizon stat arb, mid-frequency cross-sectional equity, the systematic factor manager, and agency execution. (03-algorithms/there-is-no-single-algorithm.md)

front: Where does the edge usually live in a quant pipeline?
back: Rarely in one clever model: in the joints between stages (forecast and cost model, fair value and quoting) and in plumbing such as point-in-time data, risk controls and fill feedback. (03-algorithms/there-is-no-single-algorithm.md)

front: What do the card ID letters D, F, V, P, E, M and L stand for?
back: Data and signals, forecasting models, validation and backtesting, portfolio construction, execution, market making and HFT, live trading. (03-algorithms/algorithm-map.md)

front: Which three feedback loops close the algorithm map?
back: TCA recalibrates the cost model, live monitoring retires decaying alphas, and markouts retune quoting. (03-algorithms/algorithm-map.md)

front: Point-in-time data: which two dates does every value need, and which must a backtest key on?
back: The period it describes and the moment it became public. Backtests must key on the second, via an as-of join plus a safety lag. (03-algorithms/a-data-and-signals/point-in-time-data-and-cleaning.md)

front: The four errors behind most fake alpha in data?
back: As-restated fundamentals, missing dead stocks, unadjusted corporate actions and broken identifier maps. (03-algorithms/a-data-and-signals/point-in-time-data-and-cleaning.md)

front: Number: standard delisting-return imputations, and what the fix does to the Nasdaq size effect?
back: -30% for NYSE/Amex (Shumway 1997) and -55% for Nasdaq (Shumway and Warther 1999). With the fix, the Nasdaq size effect vanishes. (03-algorithms/a-data-and-signals/point-in-time-data-and-cleaning.md)

front: Define an as-of join.
back: For each stock and decision time, take the latest record public strictly before the decision, plus a safety lag. (03-algorithms/a-data-and-signals/point-in-time-data-and-cleaning.md)

front: Define a feature in quant equity research.
back: One number per stock per timestamp, built only from data public before the decision, that might predict the target return. (03-algorithms/a-data-and-signals/feature-engineering.md)

front: Which feature families dominated in Gu, Kelly and Xiu (2020)?
back: Momentum, liquidity and volatility. (03-algorithms/a-data-and-signals/feature-engineering.md)

front: What makes a good feature, and what do more features mostly add?
back: Scale-free, correctly lagged, relative to peers and robust to outliers. More features mostly add leakage risk and multiple testing, not alpha. (03-algorithms/a-data-and-signals/feature-engineering.md)

front: Signal transforms: winsorize or z-score first, and why?
back: Winsorize first; otherwise one bad print sets everyone's scale. (03-algorithms/a-data-and-signals/signal-transforms.md)

front: What is neutralization, and its Lab 11 effect?
back: A per-date regression of the signal on beta, industries and styles, keeping the residual. Lab 11: it lifted a winsorized signal's IC from 0.019 to 0.025 (synthetic lab result). (03-algorithms/a-data-and-signals/signal-transforms.md)

front: Formula: Grinold's conversion of a score into an expected return?
back: alpha = IC x volatility x score (Grinold 1994). Optimizers need expected returns, not ranks. (03-algorithms/a-data-and-signals/signal-transforms.md)

front: What does smoothing a signal trade off?
back: A little IC for much less turnover; a common choice is an EWMA half-life about equal to the signal's half-life. (03-algorithms/a-data-and-signals/signal-transforms.md)

front: Define the information coefficient (IC).
back: Each day's cross-sectional (usually rank) correlation of the signal with subsequent residual returns. Its noise is about 1/sqrt(N): 0.045 at 500 names. (03-algorithms/a-data-and-signals/evaluating-signals.md)

front: Number: typical daily IC of one real signal?
back: About 0.005-0.03; 0.05 is exceptional and above 0.1 is usually a bug [Lore]. (03-algorithms/a-data-and-signals/evaluating-signals.md)

front: How does mean IC relate to Sharpe?
back: Mean IC / its standard deviation, annualized (x sqrt(252)), approximates the pre-cost Sharpe: the Fundamental Law in disguise. (03-algorithms/a-data-and-signals/evaluating-signals.md)

front: Why do overlapping returns need Newey-West t-stats? (Lab 11)
back: Overlapping multi-day returns are autocorrelated and inflate naive t-stats: Lab 11 showed naive 45 vs Newey-West 25 (synthetic). Use lags of horizon minus 1. (03-algorithms/a-data-and-signals/evaluating-signals.md)

front: When does a new signal earn a positive weight in an existing book?
back: Only if its IR exceeds its correlation with the book times the book's IR. (03-algorithms/a-data-and-signals/evaluating-signals.md)

front: Number: how predictable are stock returns (Gu, Kelly and Xiu 2020)?
back: The best monthly stock-level out-of-sample R-squared was 0.40%; daily, 0.05-0.25% is good [Estimate]. At that signal-to-noise ratio estimation variance dominates. (03-algorithms/b-forecasting-models/linear-models-and-regularization.md)

front: Why do shrunk coefficients (ridge, lasso) beat OLS for return forecasting?
back: Returns are mostly noise, so estimation variance dominates bias; shrinkage trades a little bias for much less variance. (03-algorithms/b-forecasting-models/linear-models-and-regularization.md)

front: How should the ridge or lasso penalty be chosen?
back: By purged walk-forward cross-validation on rank IC, never by random K-fold. (03-algorithms/b-forecasting-models/linear-models-and-regularization.md)

front: Pooled versus Fama-MacBeth (per-date) regressions differ mainly in what?
back: How they weight dates. (03-algorithms/b-forecasting-models/linear-models-and-regularization.md)

front: Number: trees versus OLS in Gu, Kelly and Xiu (2020)?
back: Trees and neural nets reached monthly out-of-sample R-squared of 0.33-0.40% vs 0.16% for a three-characteristic OLS; the gains came from nonlinear interactions. (03-algorithms/b-forecasting-models/tree-ensembles.md)

front: What do winning gradient-boosting settings look like for stock data?
back: Deliberately weak: shallow trees (15-63 leaves), learning rates 0.01-0.05, big leaves (min_data_in_leaf 500-5,000), subsampling, early stopping on time-ordered validation. (03-algorithms/b-forecasting-models/tree-ensembles.md)

front: Spot the error: "Gain-based feature importance tells you which signals drive the model."
back: Gain-based importance misleads, and SHAP still splits credit among substitutes. Target engineering often matters more than hyperparameters. (03-algorithms/b-forecasting-models/tree-ensembles.md)

front: Tree ensembles: two failure modes beyond overfitting?
back: No extrapolation beyond the training range, and jumpy forecasts that raise turnover (plus early stopping on a random split). (03-algorithms/b-forecasting-models/tree-ensembles.md)

front: Neural nets in quant: the two distinct uses?
back: Feed-forward nets (MLPs) on stock characteristics, and sequence models (CNN, LSTM, transformer) on order-book data for seconds-ahead moves; DeepLOB (2019) is the reference. (03-algorithms/b-forecasting-models/neural-nets-and-sequence-models.md)

front: Why are seed ensembles standard for neural-net forecasters?
back: Low signal-to-noise, nonstationary data make single nets vary by random seed; averaging 5-10 seeds stabilizes forecasts. (03-algorithms/b-forecasting-models/neural-nets-and-sequence-models.md)

front: How do HFT firms fit neural nets into a microsecond budget?
back: Train on GPUs overnight; hot-path models are tiny, quantized or distilled, using roughly 1 microsecond or less of tick-to-trade [Estimate]. (03-algorithms/b-forecasting-models/neural-nets-and-sequence-models.md)

front: What do LLMs mainly do in production quant?
back: Turn text (news, filings, call transcripts) into features for ordinary forecasting models, and serve as coding and research tools. (03-algorithms/b-forecasting-models/llms-and-foundation-models-in-quant.md)

front: What is the central problem in backtesting LLM signals?
back: Look-ahead leakage: a model trained on text through year Y has read what happened next. Only post-cutoff backtests are clean. (03-algorithms/b-forecasting-models/llms-and-foundation-models-in-quant.md)

front: Spot the error: "Off-the-shelf time-series foundation models beat boosted trees on daily stock returns."
back: Chronos and TimesFM forecast generic series well zero-shot, but off the shelf they trail boosted trees on daily stock returns. (03-algorithms/b-forecasting-models/llms-and-foundation-models-in-quant.md)

front: Key LLM signal parameters for point-in-time hygiene?
back: A pinned model version, temperature 0, fixed prompt and answer format, and news-to-session mapping (after 16:00 ET goes to the next open). (03-algorithms/b-forecasting-models/llms-and-foundation-models-in-quant.md)

front: The alpha-combination ladder?
back: Equal weight, IC weighting, ridge or mean-variance on the alpha covariance, then nonlinear meta-models. Each rung estimates more parameters. (03-algorithms/b-forecasting-models/alpha-combination-and-ensembling.md)

front: Where does ridge sit between mean-variance and IC weighting? (Lab 12)
back: Ridge tends to mean-variance as lambda goes to 0 and to IC weighting as lambda grows. Lab 12: out-of-sample IC 0.085 vs oracle 0.087; equal weight 0.050 (synthetic). (03-algorithms/b-forecasting-models/alpha-combination-and-ensembling.md)

front: Spot the error: "IC weighting is safe with correlated signals."
back: IC weighting double-counts correlated signals. Also weight fast-decaying signals by the alpha that survives costs, not raw IC. (03-algorithms/b-forecasting-models/alpha-combination-and-ensembling.md)

front: Regime detection: what is it, and how do firms mostly use it?
back: Estimating each day the probability of persistent states (calm, stressed) from data available that day. Mostly defensively: to scale risk or gate strategies, rarely to forecast returns. (03-algorithms/b-forecasting-models/regime-detection.md)

front: What is the hindsight trap in regime detection?
back: Smoothed state probabilities and official recession dates use future data; a live model can only use filtered, as-of-that-day probabilities. Evidence that regime timing pays is contested. (03-algorithms/b-forecasting-models/regime-detection.md)

front: Typical regime-model parameters?
back: 2-3 states; daily stay probability 0.95-0.99 (average spells of 20-100 days); vol lookback 20-63 days; VIX trigger 25-30; a hysteresis band. (03-algorithms/b-forecasting-models/regime-detection.md)

front: Why does shuffled K-fold fail on financial data?
back: Labels overlap (a daily-sampled 5-day return shares 4 days with its neighbor) and features persist, so shuffling leaks near-copies of test rows into training. (03-algorithms/c-validation-and-backtesting/time-series-cross-validation.md)

front: Define purging and embargo.
back: Purging drops training dates whose labels overlap test labels (purge = label horizon h). An embargo drops data just after each test block, about 1% of the sample (Lopez de Prado 2018). (03-algorithms/c-validation-and-backtesting/time-series-cross-validation.md)

front: Number: Lab 12's leakage by validation scheme?
back: GBDT out-of-sample IC 0.127 under shuffled K-fold, 0.066 walk-forward, 0.076 purged; ridge leaked only 0.002. The leak scales with model flexibility (synthetic). (03-algorithms/c-validation-and-backtesting/time-series-cross-validation.md)

front: What does combinatorial purged CV (CPCV) add over walk-forward?
back: Many backtest paths instead of one, from combinations of test groups (e.g., 6-10 groups, 2 for test), each purged and embargoed. (03-algorithms/c-validation-and-backtesting/time-series-cross-validation.md)

front: Why is model selection statistically slow?
back: Separating two models whose ICs differ by 0.005 can take about three years of test data (illustrative). Tune hyperparameters in inner folds (nested CV). (03-algorithms/c-validation-and-backtesting/time-series-cross-validation.md)

front: Vectorized versus event-driven backtesters?
back: Vectorized runs decades in seconds for daily cross-sectional research. Event-driven processes one event at a time on production's code path; intraday and passive strategies need it. (03-algorithms/c-validation-and-backtesting/backtesting-engines.md)

front: Where does backtest realism live?
back: In the fill and cost model: spread, fees and rebates, impact, partial fills, queue position, latency, borrow, financing and corporate actions. (03-algorithms/c-validation-and-backtesting/backtesting-engines.md)

front: What can HFT market-replay simulators not show?
back: Others reacting to your orders. They rebuild the book and estimate queue position, but live trading is the final test. (03-algorithms/c-validation-and-backtesting/backtesting-engines.md)

front: Typical backtest cost model formula?
back: Half-spread + fees + k x sigma x sqrt(Q/ADV), with a participation cap of 5-20% of volume and borrow from 0.25% to 50%+ a year. (03-algorithms/c-validation-and-backtesting/backtesting-engines.md)

front: Which way do nearly all backtest biases push?
back: Up. Data and timing errors invent returns; cost, borrow and capacity errors inflate real ones; statistical errors inflate confidence. (03-algorithms/c-validation-and-backtesting/backtest-pitfalls.md)

front: Number: how much do published predictors decay (McLean and Pontiff 2016)?
back: Across 97 predictors, returns fall about 26% out of sample and 58% after publication. (03-algorithms/c-validation-and-backtesting/backtest-pitfalls.md)

front: Number: how well did backtest Sharpe predict live Sharpe across 888 Quantopian algorithms?
back: Backtest Sharpe explained under 2.5% of out-of-sample Sharpe. (03-algorithms/c-validation-and-backtesting/backtest-pitfalls.md)

front: Spot the error: "Haircut every backtest Sharpe by a flat 50%."
back: Harvey and Liu's haircut is nonlinear: a flat 50% is too lenient for marginal Sharpe ratios and too harsh for strong ones. Sharpe 1.0 from 100 tests (10 years) becomes 0.44. (03-algorithms/c-validation-and-backtesting/backtest-pitfalls.md)

front: Standard stress tests in a backtest audit?
back: Honest trial count, t-hurdle 3.0, 2x costs, +1 day lag, position cap 1-5% of ADV, Newey-West lags = horizon - 1. (03-algorithms/c-validation-and-backtesting/backtest-pitfalls.md)

front: Formula: how fast does the best of N zero-skill backtests improve by luck?
back: Its Sharpe grows like sqrt(2 ln N) standard errors, so trying more variants manufactures a good-looking winner. (03-algorithms/c-validation-and-backtesting/overfitting-and-multiple-testing.md)

front: Define the Deflated Sharpe Ratio and PBO.
back: DSR: probability the true Sharpe beats the luck hurdle implied by the trials (pass mark 0.95). PBO: how often the in-sample winner ends below the out-of-sample median. (03-algorithms/c-validation-and-backtesting/overfitting-and-multiple-testing.md)

front: Number: Lab 13's best-of-500 noise strategies?
back: Sharpe 2.18 in sample, -0.90 out of sample; DSR 0.34 vs 0.94 for a planted alpha; PBO 0.64 vs 0.22 (synthetic lab result). (03-algorithms/c-validation-and-backtesting/overfitting-and-multiple-testing.md)

front: What does every overfitting correction need?
back: An honest trial count, research graveyard included. (03-algorithms/c-validation-and-backtesting/overfitting-and-multiple-testing.md)

front: Formula: structure of a factor risk model?
back: Sigma = X F X' + Delta: exposures X (N x K), factor covariance F, and diagonal specific variances Delta. Millions of unknowns shrink to thousands. (03-algorithms/d-portfolio-construction/risk-models.md)

front: Three families of equity risk models?
back: Fundamental (BARRA-style industries and styles, daily cross-sectional regression), statistical (principal components) and hybrids. K is about 70-100 fundamental or 10-20 statistical factors. (03-algorithms/d-portfolio-construction/risk-models.md)

front: Define the bias statistic, and the Lab 14 lesson.
back: Std of return / forecast risk; 1 = unbiased. Grade on optimized portfolios: Lab 14's sample covariance scored 1.00 on random portfolios but 2.78 on optimized ones (synthetic). (03-algorithms/d-portfolio-construction/risk-models.md)

front: What is the alpha-risk alignment problem?
back: Alpha that the risk model cannot see looks diversifiable, so the optimizer overloads it. (03-algorithms/d-portfolio-construction/risk-models.md)

front: Why do risk models use shorter half-lives for volatilities than correlations?
back: Volatilities move fast and need responsiveness (42-252 days); correlations need many observations to estimate (200-756 days). (03-algorithms/d-portfolio-construction/risk-models.md)

front: Why is a sample covariance unusable when N rivals T?
back: It is singular when N > T (Lab 14: 500 stocks, 252 days, rank 251); near N = T small eigenvalues are too small and large ones too large, misleading the optimizer. (03-algorithms/d-portfolio-construction/covariance-estimation-and-shrinkage.md)

front: Random-matrix theory: the noise band for eigenvalues?
back: Pure-noise eigenvalues spread over (1 +/- sqrt(N/T))^2. For S&P 500 stocks, 94% of correlation eigenvalues fit such a band. (03-algorithms/d-portfolio-construction/covariance-estimation-and-shrinkage.md)

front: Four fixes for noisy covariance matrices?
back: Linear shrinkage toward a target (Ledoit-Wolf), factor models, eigenvalue clipping and nonlinear shrinkage. (03-algorithms/d-portfolio-construction/covariance-estimation-and-shrinkage.md)

front: EWMA covariance: what constraint links half-life and N?
back: Effective sample is about 2.9 half-lives and must stay well above N. RiskMetrics uses lambda = 0.94. (03-algorithms/d-portfolio-construction/covariance-estimation-and-shrinkage.md)

front: Formula: the mean-variance optimization objective?
back: Maximize alpha'w - lambda w'Sigma w - cost(w - w0) subject to constraints (neutrality, caps, leverage, % ADV, turnover). Convex: 3,000 names solve in seconds. (03-algorithms/d-portfolio-construction/mean-variance-optimization.md)

front: Why did Michaud call MVO "error maximization"?
back: Unconstrained w* = Sigma^-1 alpha / (2 lambda): a noisy inverse times noisy forecasts, so the optimizer bets hardest where estimates are most wrong. (03-algorithms/d-portfolio-construction/mean-variance-optimization.md)

front: What is the transfer coefficient, and its typical range?
back: The share of the unconstrained Fundamental Law that survives constraints: realized performance runs at 0.3-0.8 of it. (03-algorithms/d-portfolio-construction/mean-variance-optimization.md)

front: Typical MVO parameters for a quant equity book?
back: Risk aversion 5-50, cost aversion 0.25-3, name cap 0.5-3% of capital, gross 200-600%, trades capped at 5-10% of ADV. (03-algorithms/d-portfolio-construction/mean-variance-optimization.md)

front: Risk-based alternatives to MVO?
back: 1/N, inverse volatility, equal risk contribution (risk parity), minimum variance and hierarchical risk parity (HRP): they drop return forecasts. (03-algorithms/d-portfolio-construction/alternatives-to-mvo.md)

front: How does Black-Litterman tame MVO?
back: It shrinks inputs toward a prior: back out market-implied returns (pi = delta Sigma w_mkt), blend in views by confidence (tau 0.01-0.05), then run MVO. (03-algorithms/d-portfolio-construction/alternatives-to-mvo.md)

front: How should you choose between MVO and its alternatives?
back: By how much you trust your return forecasts; the 1/N debate is unresolved. Factor managers often skip the optimizer for rank-weighted books with risk controls. (03-algorithms/d-portfolio-construction/alternatives-to-mvo.md)

front: Formula: the square-root impact law?
back: Impact is about Y x sigma x sqrt(Q/V), Y of order 1 (0.5-1), sigma daily. Double the order: +41% cost per share and 2.8x the dollars. (03-algorithms/d-portfolio-construction/transaction-cost-and-impact-models.md)

front: Number: buying 5% of ADV in a 2%-daily-vol stock?
back: Peak impact 22.4-44.7 bps (Y 0.5-1); the average fill pays two-thirds of the peak, 14.9-29.8 bps; plus a few bps of spread and commission (illustrative). (03-algorithms/d-portfolio-construction/transaction-cost-and-impact-models.md)

front: What are the components of a pre-trade cost model?
back: Fees + half-spread + market impact, plus borrow and the opportunity cost of skipped trades. The optimizer nets it against alpha. (03-algorithms/d-portfolio-construction/transaction-cost-and-impact-models.md)

front: Spot the error: "Academic impact estimates are the right default for a large quant manager."
back: Calibrate on your own fills: AQR's live trades cost an order of magnitude less than academic estimates. Watch for alpha leaking into the calibration. (03-algorithms/d-portfolio-construction/transaction-cost-and-impact-models.md)

front: Garleanu and Pedersen (2013) in one sentence?
back: Aim in front of the target, and trade partially toward the aim. (03-algorithms/d-portfolio-construction/multi-period-and-trading-toward-aim.md)

front: What determines the trade rate toward the aim?
back: Costs and risk aversion, not alpha decay. Lab 15's grid search recovered the closed-form 0.213 within about 2% (synthetic). (03-algorithms/d-portfolio-construction/multi-period-and-trading-toward-aim.md)

front: How does the aim treat fast-decaying signals? (Lab 15)
back: It shrinks them: a 60-day-half-life signal keeps 96% of its weight, a 1-day signal 35%. Fully rebalancing a 1-day signal daily nets Sharpe -17.5 (synthetic). (03-algorithms/d-portfolio-construction/multi-period-and-trading-toward-aim.md)

front: What do linear costs and constraints do to the Garleanu-Pedersen solution?
back: Linear costs add no-trade bands; constraints break the closed form, so desks solve multi-period convex problems. (03-algorithms/d-portfolio-construction/multi-period-and-trading-toward-aim.md)

front: Formula: Kelly fraction and growth rate?
back: f* = mu / sigma^2; growth = f mu - f^2 sigma^2 / 2. Example: 7% excess return at 10% vol gives 7x leverage; half Kelly keeps 75% of the growth at half the vol. (03-algorithms/d-portfolio-construction/position-sizing-and-risk-budgeting.md)

front: Why do practitioners run a quarter to half Kelly?
back: Kelly needs the true Sharpe; at twice true Kelly growth is zero, and Sharpe estimates are usually overstated. (03-algorithms/d-portfolio-construction/position-sizing-and-risk-budgeting.md)

front: Formula and typical target for volatility targeting?
back: w = target vol / forecast vol (EWMA); 10% a year is a common target [Lore]. Lab 19: rolling vol 7.0-12.3% vs 4.9-16.7% for equal notional (5th-95th percentile, synthetic). (03-algorithms/d-portfolio-construction/position-sizing-and-risk-budgeting.md)

front: When do stop-losses help (Kaminski and Lo 2014)?
back: When returns trend (momentum); under a random walk they cost money. (03-algorithms/d-portfolio-construction/position-sizing-and-risk-budgeting.md)

front: The three layers of an execution algorithm?
back: Scheduler (how much by when), placement (post or take, size, price) and smart order router (where). (03-algorithms/e-execution-algorithms/execution-algorithms-overview.md)

front: What mainly distinguishes execution algo families?
back: The benchmark they chase: TWAP, VWAP, POV, implementation shortfall (arrival), target close, liquidity-seeking, pegged. Choose by size (% ADV), urgency and benchmark. (03-algorithms/e-execution-algorithms/execution-algorithms-overview.md)

front: Number: expected cost versus risk in Lab 17 (10% of ADV in a day)?
back: Expected cost 12.8-17.9 bps by schedule against shortfall standard deviations of 122-180 bps (synthetic): risk dwarfs cost differences. (03-algorithms/e-execution-algorithms/execution-algorithms-overview.md)

front: Number: algo and algo-wheel usage on US buy-side desks (FY2025)?
back: Algos and smart order routers carried 43% of US buy-side equity activity; 36% of desks use algo wheels [Reported]. (03-algorithms/e-execution-algorithms/execution-algorithms-overview.md)

front: TWAP versus VWAP versus POV?
back: TWAP slices by the clock, VWAP by a forecast volume curve, POV by live volume. A VWAP engine is mostly a volume forecaster. (03-algorithms/e-execution-algorithms/vwap-twap-pov.md)

front: Number: Lab 17 expected costs by schedule?
back: VWAP 12.8 bps, POV 13.1, TWAP 14.0 (synthetic, 10% of ADV in a day). POV finished the order on only 61% of days. (03-algorithms/e-execution-algorithms/vwap-twap-pov.md)

front: Spot the error: "Beating VWAP proves good execution."
back: The VWAP benchmark is easy to hit by trading with the market and hides about a third of the true cost; measure against arrival price. (03-algorithms/e-execution-algorithms/vwap-twap-pov.md)

front: Define implementation shortfall.
back: Execution cost against the decision price, unfilled shares included (Perold 1988). It captures delay, spread, impact and opportunity cost. (03-algorithms/e-execution-algorithms/implementation-shortfall-and-almgren-chriss.md)

front: Almgren-Chriss: objective and solution shape?
back: Minimize E[IS] + lambda Var[IS]. Holdings decay like sinh(kappa(T - t)) / sinh(kappa T), kappa about sqrt(lambda sigma^2 / eta); lambda = 0 is TWAP. Impact punishes speed, risk punishes waiting. (03-algorithms/e-execution-algorithms/implementation-shortfall-and-almgren-chriss.md)

front: Number: Lab 16's $500M order at 50% of a $1B ADV over 5 days?
back: TWAP expects 46 bps with a 254 bp standard deviation; a risk-averse schedule 96 bps with SD 110 (synthetic). (03-algorithms/e-execution-algorithms/implementation-shortfall-and-almgren-chriss.md)

front: Why do linear-impact Almgren-Chriss models overstate the cost of speed?
back: Under square-root impact the fastest schedule costs 84 bps, not the linear model's 242 (Lab 16). Also, on single orders TWAP beat the risk-averse schedule 61% of the time. (03-algorithms/e-execution-algorithms/implementation-shortfall-and-almgren-chriss.md)

front: What does a smart order router minimize?
back: All-in cost per child order: spread + fees - rebates + markout + non-fill cleanup, by choosing venue, order type, size and sequence. (03-algorithms/e-execution-algorithms/smart-order-routing.md)

front: How does an aggressive SOR take liquidity?
back: It pings dark midpoint pools, then sweeps every protected quote at once with intermarket sweep orders (ISOs). (03-algorithms/e-execution-algorithms/smart-order-routing.md)

front: Spot the error: "Route passive orders to the venues with the highest fill rates."
back: High fill rates often signal toxicity. Lab 18: a fill-chasing router cost 2.83 bps vs 1.48 for a markout-aware bandit (synthetic). (03-algorithms/e-execution-algorithms/smart-order-routing.md)

front: Closing-auction cutoffs and the post-cutoff rule?
back: New MOC/LOC orders stop at 3:50 p.m. (NYSE) and 3:55 p.m. (Nasdaq). After the cutoff you may only add on the side that offsets the imbalance, exactly when the auction pays a concession. (03-algorithms/e-execution-algorithms/auction-close-and-dark-liquidity-algos.md)

front: How do dark algos avoid being picked off?
back: Midpoint pegs and conditional orders across pools with minimum fill sizes against probing; venues are judged by markouts, not fill rates. (03-algorithms/e-execution-algorithms/auction-close-and-dark-liquidity-algos.md)

front: What is the hidden cost of dark trading, with an enforcement example?
back: Information leakage. One dark-pool operator paid $84.3M to settle charges. (03-algorithms/e-execution-algorithms/auction-close-and-dark-liquidity-algos.md)

front: TCA in accounting terms?
back: Variance analysis for trading: pre-trade forecasts cost and picks the strategy; post-trade measures, attributes to owners (delay, spread, market move, impact and timing, opportunity cost, fees) and recalibrates. (03-algorithms/e-execution-algorithms/transaction-cost-analysis.md)

front: Why can one order not rank brokers?
back: Per-order standard deviations of 50-150 bps dwarf broker differences of a few bps, so comparisons need hundreds to thousands of orders, randomized allocation (algo wheels) and market adjustment. (03-algorithms/e-execution-algorithms/transaction-cost-analysis.md)

front: The stages of an HFT event loop?
back: Packet in, book update, fair value, quote decision, risk check, order out. Acks and fills return later and update inventory and hedges. (03-algorithms/f-market-making-and-hft-algorithms/anatomy-of-an-hft-trading-loop.md)

front: Number: state-of-the-art tick-to-trade?
back: About 2.5 microseconds in very good software; tens of nanoseconds on FPGAs [Verified]. Rank in the race matters more than absolute speed. (03-algorithms/f-market-making-and-hft-algorithms/anatomy-of-an-hft-trading-loop.md)

front: Why is an HFT core single-threaded and deterministic, with models fit offline?
back: So a recorded day replays to identical orders, and the hot path only does arithmetic and lookups on parameters pushed from offline fits. (03-algorithms/f-market-making-and-hft-algorithms/anatomy-of-an-hft-trading-loop.md)

front: Weighted mid versus microprice?
back: The weighted mid leans toward the thin side by imbalance x half-spread; Stoikov's microprice (2018) learns how much of that lean actually comes true. (03-algorithms/f-market-making-and-hft-algorithms/fair-value-and-microprice.md)

front: Number: Lab 02's fair-value comparison?
back: Microprice cut next-move forecast error only 3.5% vs the mid; the weighted mid was 41% worse. Past about 10 seconds nothing book-based beats the mid (synthetic). (03-algorithms/f-market-making-and-hft-algorithms/fair-value-and-microprice.md)

front: Spot the error: "The order book contains the information a market maker needs for fair value."
back: The book is not the information: real fair values add trade flow and futures or ETF leads, each shrunk (leader shrinkage about 0.3-0.7 [Lore]). (03-algorithms/f-market-making-and-hft-algorithms/fair-value-and-microprice.md)

front: Cont, Kukanov and Stoikov (2014): OFI result?
back: Over 10-second intervals the mid change is about OFI / (2 x depth); OFI explained 65% of price variance, trade imbalance 32% (50 S&P 500 stocks). (03-algorithms/f-market-making-and-hft-algorithms/order-book-and-trade-flow-signals.md)

front: Explaining versus predicting with OFI (Lab 03)?
back: OFI explained 70% of the same 10-second move but only 4.5% of the next one (synthetic). A same-interval fit is not a forecast. (03-algorithms/f-market-making-and-hft-algorithms/order-book-and-trade-flow-signals.md)

front: Who monetizes order-flow signals, takers or makers?
back: Market makers, for free, to skew and cancel quotes. Lab 03's taker lost 1.44 ticks per round trip (synthetic). (03-algorithms/f-market-making-and-hft-algorithms/order-book-and-trade-flow-signals.md)

front: Formula: Avellaneda-Stoikov reservation price and spread?
back: r = s - q gamma sigma^2 (T - t); spread = gamma sigma^2 (T - t) + (2/gamma) ln(1 + gamma/k). Long inventory (q > 0) shades both quotes down. (03-algorithms/f-market-making-and-hft-algorithms/quoting-and-inventory-control.md)

front: What does GLFT (Gueant, Lehalle and Fernandez-Tapia 2013) add to Avellaneda-Stoikov?
back: Closed-form, clock-free quotes with inventory limits, leaning a constant amount per lot. (03-algorithms/f-market-making-and-hft-algorithms/quoting-and-inventory-control.md)

front: Number: Lab 05 quoting results?
back: GLFT earned what naive quoting earned ($95 vs $94 an hour) at a fifth of the risk; adverse selection cut it to $42; faster stale-quote cancels lifted it to $68; widening barely helped (synthetic). (03-algorithms/f-market-making-and-hft-algorithms/quoting-and-inventory-control.md)

front: What matters more than the quoting formula in practice?
back: Fair value and an adverse-selection floor (floor = expected markout + fees) [Lore]. (03-algorithms/f-market-making-and-hft-algorithms/quoting-and-inventory-control.md)

front: Glosten-Milgrom intuition for the spread?
back: Whoever chooses to hit your quote knows more on average; the uninformed pay a spread that covers losses to the informed. (03-algorithms/f-market-making-and-hft-algorithms/adverse-selection-and-markouts.md)

front: Formula: a markout?
back: side x (mid at t + h - fill price). At h = 0 it is the spread captured; the fall after that is adverse selection. (03-algorithms/f-market-making-and-hft-algorithms/adverse-selection-and-markouts.md)

front: Number: Lab 04 informed versus noise markouts?
back: Informed flow looked profitable at 1 s but ended at -1.46 bps at 60 s; noise flow ended at +2.13 bps (synthetic). (03-algorithms/f-market-making-and-hft-algorithms/adverse-selection-and-markouts.md)

front: Markouts: common measurement mistakes?
back: Horizon too short, per-fill instead of per-share averaging, naive standard errors (fills cluster), fees omitted, and seeing only the fills you got. (03-algorithms/f-market-making-and-hft-algorithms/adverse-selection-and-markouts.md)

front: Formula: value of a resting order?
back: P(fill) x (half-spread + rebate + markout). Both terms worsen with every share queued ahead of you. (03-algorithms/f-market-making-and-hft-algorithms/queue-position-and-order-placement.md)

front: Number: what is queue priority worth in a large-tick stock (Lab 01)?
back: About half a tick: $0.56 per 100 shares (synthetic), above a market maker's net margin. (03-algorithms/f-market-making-and-hft-algorithms/queue-position-and-order-placement.md)

front: How do you know your queue position?
back: Exactly with order-level (MBO) feeds; with level-only (MBP) feeds it is a guess about where cancels came from. (03-algorithms/f-market-making-and-hft-algorithms/queue-position-and-order-placement.md)

front: Spot the error: "Hedging more often raises expected P&L."
back: More frequent rebalancing shrinks hedge-error variance but, before costs, not expected P&L; costs then fall on expected P&L. Lab 06: 15-minute hedging cost more than the quoted edge. (03-algorithms/f-market-making-and-hft-algorithms/hedging-algorithms.md)

front: Three hedge-timing rules?
back: A clock, a band on net delta, or a utility-optimal band (Whalley-Wilmott). (03-algorithms/f-market-making-and-hft-algorithms/hedging-algorithms.md)

front: Hedging: net or gross, and which instrument?
back: Net across books first, then hedge in the cheapest correlated instrument at a minimum-variance ratio; only options hedge gamma and vega. (03-algorithms/f-market-making-and-hft-algorithms/hedging-algorithms.md)

front: Formula: gamma P&L of a delta-hedged option?
back: dPi is about (1/2) Gamma S^2 (implied variance - realized variance) dt for the short side: it earns theta and pays gamma. Long side: flip the sign. (03-algorithms/f-market-making-and-hft-algorithms/hedging-algorithms.md)

front: Spot the error: "Options market makers price with Black-Scholes."
back: Black-Scholes is the quoting language, not the model: prices become implied vols. The model is the fitted volatility surface (SVI, spline or SABR smiles, checked for static arbitrage). (03-algorithms/f-market-making-and-hft-algorithms/options-pricing-and-vol-surfaces-for-mm.md)

front: The two speeds of an options pricing engine?
back: Refit the surface every second to minute; reprice thousands of series on every underlying tick under a sticky-strike or sticky-delta rule. (03-algorithms/f-market-making-and-hft-algorithms/options-pricing-and-vol-surfaces-for-mm.md)

front: Number: wing fit error, parabola versus SVI (Lab 06)?
back: A parabola missed the wings by 1.25 vol points, SVI by 0.12 (synthetic). (03-algorithms/f-market-making-and-hft-algorithms/options-pricing-and-vol-surfaces-for-mm.md)

front: What does SEC Rule 15c3-5 (2010) require?
back: Broker-dealers with market access must automatically reject orders that breach pre-set credit or capital thresholds or price and size limits, or that look duplicative. (03-algorithms/f-market-making-and-hft-algorithms/algorithmic-risk-controls.md)

front: Number: Knight Capital, 1 August 2012?
back: 212 retail orders became over 4 million executions in 154 stocks in 45 minutes; loss over $460 million [Verified]. (03-algorithms/f-market-making-and-hft-algorithms/algorithmic-risk-controls.md)

front: Design principle for risk controls: strict or generous?
back: Strict on the way in, generous on the way out: cancels and risk-reducing orders always pass. Layers (strategy, gateway, exchange port, market-wide) each assume the previous failed. (03-algorithms/f-market-making-and-hft-algorithms/algorithmic-risk-controls.md)

front: Name two classic risk-control failure modes.
back: Limits that only alert; account-level instead of firm-wide limits; false kills; a kill switch that strands hedges. (03-algorithms/f-market-making-and-hft-algorithms/algorithmic-risk-controls.md)

front: Quant equity P&L attribution formula?
back: P&L = sum(dollar factor exposure x factor return) + specific P&L + trading P&L. Alpha should appear in the specific line. (03-algorithms/g-live-trading/live-monitoring-and-pnl-attribution.md)

front: Market-maker P&L as an income statement?
back: Spread capture + rebates - adverse selection +/- inventory - hedging costs - fees. (03-algorithms/g-live-trading/live-monitoring-and-pnl-attribution.md)

front: Typical live-monitoring alert bands?
back: P&L beyond 3 sigma of ex-ante risk, slippage over 1.5-2x the cost model, limit usage above 80%. (03-algorithms/g-live-trading/live-monitoring-and-pnl-attribution.md)

front: Formula: standard error of a Sharpe ratio, and what it implies?
back: SE is about sqrt((1 + SR^2/2) / T) in per-period units, roughly 1/sqrt(years). Separating Sharpe 1.0 from 0 at two standard errors takes about four years. (03-algorithms/g-live-trading/alpha-decay-detection-and-model-retirement.md)

front: How do firms detect alpha decay?
back: They stack weak evidence: rolling IC t-stats, a CUSUM alarm on signal P&L, a Bayesian Sharpe posterior (backtest haircut 30-60%), crowding and capacity checks. (03-algorithms/g-live-trading/alpha-decay-detection-and-model-retirement.md)

front: How is a decaying model retired?
back: In stages (watch, down-weight, freeze, retire); alarms trigger a human review, not an automatic kill. (03-algorithms/g-live-trading/alpha-decay-detection-and-model-retirement.md)

front: Why do execution, market making and hedging suit reinforcement learning?
back: Today's action changes tomorrow's state: inventory carries over, so a policy maximizing cumulative reward fits. (03-algorithms/g-live-trading/reinforcement-learning-in-trading.md)

front: Why is RL hard in trading?
back: Markets are non-stationary, simulators cannot show how the market reacts to you, agents exploit simulator flaws, and there is one history to learn from. (03-algorithms/g-live-trading/reinforcement-learning-in-trading.md)

front: Where is RL reported in production?
back: Mainly bank execution (J.P. Morgan's LOXM, 2017); deep hedging was co-developed by J.P. Morgan researchers. RL as a quant-fund profit engine is lore. (03-algorithms/g-live-trading/reinforcement-learning-in-trading.md)

front: Stat-arb walkthrough: why did the traded day lose $48K?
back: $68K of expected alpha was swamped by $55K of stock-specific noise, $49K of factor losses and $13K of costs. Single days are mostly noise (synthetic). (03-algorithms/h-end-to-end-walkthroughs/walkthrough-mid-frequency-stat-arb.md)

front: Stat-arb walkthrough: two-year result, and the reality check?
back: $17.9M gross and $14.6M net a year on $100M, Sharpe 12.5 and 10.3: a stylized synthetic lab result; real books of this design net roughly 1-2 [Lore]. (03-algorithms/h-end-to-end-walkthroughs/walkthrough-mid-frequency-stat-arb.md)

front: Three lessons of the stat-arb walkthrough?
back: Neutralize on the beta you actually trade, judge a risk model on the optimized book, and let costs decide how far to trade. (03-algorithms/h-end-to-end-walkthroughs/walkthrough-mid-frequency-stat-arb.md)

front: ETF market-maker walkthrough: the day's net trading income?
back: $10,284, or 2.35 bps of $43.8M traded: $14,142 of spread, most given back to pick-offs, hedging, basket and fees; a lucky $4,292 basis gain (synthetic). (03-algorithms/h-end-to-end-walkthroughs/walkthrough-etf-market-maker.md)

front: ETF walkthrough: why lean quotes on post-hedge risk?
back: Risk left after the futures hedge is 0.10 bp per creation unit versus 0.70 bp unhedged, so the lean should reflect the residual, not gross, inventory. (03-algorithms/h-end-to-end-walkthroughs/walkthrough-etf-market-maker.md)

front: ETF walkthrough: why measure a hedged block's markout against the hedge?
back: The raw markout is mostly market noise (+20 bps at 60 s, -34 bps by the close); against the futures hedge it stays near +8 to +11 bps, close to the spread charged. (03-algorithms/h-end-to-end-walkthroughs/walkthrough-etf-market-maker.md)
